item.title: The Bitter Lesson of BF16 Master Weights: How Small-LR RL Silently Eats Your Updates
item.description:
TL;DR

  • The Trap: Storing master weights in bfloat16 during small-learning-rate RL (lr = 5e-7) silently freezes most of the model. For a typical weight $|w| \approx 0.02$, the smallest step bf16 can resolve (half-ULP) is $6.10 \times 10^{-5}$—over $120\times$ larger than a 5e-7 Adam update. Every step rounds straight back to the original value.
  • Why It Goes Unnoticed: Training does not crash or flatline. Tiny-magnitude weights ($|w| \le 10^{-4}$) and near-zero biases have much smaller ULPs and do update—causing reward and easier benchmarks (GSM8K: 35.25% → 57.01%) to climb slowly while harder reasoning (MATH500: 35.01% → 35.01%) stays frozen at the exact untrained baseline.
  • The Fix: Restoring standard fp32 master weights (keeping bf16 forward/backward compute) beat 929 steps of bf16 training by Step 100, finishing +7.2 points higher on MATH500 (42.25%) and +21.3 points higher on GSM8K (78.32%), at the cost of ~7 GB/GPU extra memory and +20% step time.

The blog is co-authored with Gemini Carbon.

item.title: Understanding TPM, RPM, TPS, and TTFT in LLM APIs
item.description:
When working with Large Language Model (LLM) APIs, several metrics are commonly used to describe rate limits, throughput, and latency.

Understanding these metrics is essential for optimizing API performance, managing costs, and building scalable LLM applications, especially AI agents and large-scale inference systems.

1. Key Metrics at a Glance

Metric Full Name Meaning
TPM Tokens Per Minute Maximum tokens processed per minute
RPM Requests Per Minute Maximum API requests per minute
TPS Tokens Per Second Typically, token generation speed or throughput
TTFT Time to First Token Latency before the first output token arrives

These metrics describe different aspects of LLM API performance.

item.title: Cache Hits in LLMs
item.description:
The note is generated by Gemini.

Overview

In the context of Large Language Models (LLMs), a Cache Hit occurs when the inference engine identifies that specific data (tokens, KV pairs, or full responses) from a previous request is already stored in memory.

🚀 Key Types of Cache Hits

1. KV (Key-Value) Cache Hit

  • Level: Inference Engine (e.g., vLLM, TensorRT-LLM).
  • Mechanism: During the “Prefill” stage, the model stores the Key and Value tensors of the attention mechanism.
  • The Hit: Reuses stored tensors for identical prefixes.
  • Result: Drastically reduces Time to First Token (TTFT).

2. Semantic Cache Hit

  • Level: Application Layer.
  • Mechanism: Uses Vector Embeddings to compare queries.
  • The Hit: Returns a saved answer if the meaning is the same.
  • Result: Zero GPU cost and near-zero latency.

📊 Comparison Table

Metric Cache Hit Cache Miss
Computation Low (Retrieval) High (Full Forward Pass)
Latency Milliseconds Seconds
Cost Negligible Full Token Usage
Tip

Maximizing your Cache Hit Ratio is the most effective way to scale LLM apps.
